title: Troubleshooting ladders, captures, and debug
summary: Match Call-ID, CSeq, Via branch, and To tag, then read captures and IOS debug as themselves.

lessons.title: Match a ladder before you change anything
lessons.summary: A ladder is one dialog only after Call-ID, CSeq, the Via branch, and the To tag agree.
objectives: Match messages that belong to one dialog
Separate a Via branch from a dialog
Say where a 2xx ACK travels

illustration.title: Four fields that tie a ladder
illustration.caption: Read these before you rename a header or change a route.

layers.name: Call-ID
layers.detail: Same value on every hop of this dialog

layers.name: CSeq
layers.detail: Number plus method. ACK uses the INVITE number.

layers.name: Via branch
layers.detail: Identifies one transaction on one hop

layers.name: To tag
layers.detail: Absent on the first request. Present once the dialog exists.

sections.h: Match the dialog, then the transaction
paragraphs: Start with Call-ID. Every request and response in this dialog carries the same Call-ID. CSeq is a number and a method: the INVITE that opened the dialog, the responses to it, and the ACK that completes a 2xx all share that number, while the method token changes. A later re-INVITE uses a higher CSeq number.

The Via branch identifies a single transaction on a single hop. The magic cookie z9hG4bK is how you spot a branch that claims to follow RFC 3261. The To tag is empty on the initial request and present on responses that form the dialog. Matching a response to a request means Call-ID, CSeq, and the Via branch you sent, and then the To tag tells you the dialog exists.

The ACK that follows a 200 OK is end to end. It is its own request, it uses a new Via branch, and it is routed toward the Contact from the 200 OK. RFC 3261 defines that split. RFC 6026 corrects how transactions handle 2xx responses to INVITE, including the ACK that belongs with them.

The ACK that follows a non-2xx final response is hop by hop. It uses the same Via branch as the INVITE it acknowledges, and the previous hop consumes it. When you draw a ladder, label those two ACKs differently. A B2BUA may show you two dialogs; match each leg on its own Call-ID before you decide an ACK is missing.

RFC 3665 is a set of basic call-flow examples. Use it as a shape for the arrows, then trust the headers in the capture you actually have. A clean ladder names the parties, the method or status, and one sentence about why that hop matters.

Change a route, a codec list, or a timer only after the ladder says which hop failed. If Call-ID differs, you are looking at two calls. If the branch differs, you are looking at a new transaction. If the To tag is missing on a response that claims to be in-dialog, the dialog was never formed.

quiz.q: Which field identifies one transaction on one hop?
quiz.why: Call-ID groups the dialog. The branch groups the transaction hop.

quiz.q: The ACK after 200 OK travels
choices: End to end, with its own branch
Hop by hop, on the INVITE branch
Only as far as the first proxy
quiz.why: RFC 3261 separates that ACK from the hop-by-hop ACK used for non-2xx finals. RFC 6026 fixes the 2xx transaction handling.

quiz.q: The ACK after 487 travels
choices: Hop by hop on the INVITE branch
End to end like a 2xx ACK
As a response, not a request
quiz.why: Non-2xx ACKs are part of the INVITE transaction and stop at the next hop.

quiz.q: A To tag on the initial INVITE means
choices: This request is already in a dialog
quiz.why: A To tag on a request means an existing dialog. A brand-new INVITE omits it.

quiz.q: 100 Trying tells you
choices: This hop received the INVITE and will retransmit less often
quiz.why: 100 is hop-by-hop and provisional. Ringing is 180.

quiz.q: RFC 3665 is useful here because it
quiz.why: Use it as a picture. The headers in your capture still win.

cards.back: Same value for the dialog. A B2BUA may use a new one on the other leg.
Integer plus method. The ACK for an INVITE keeps the INVITE's number.
Transaction hop id. Look for the z9hG4bK cookie.
End to end. New branch. RFC 6026 corrects the transaction rules around it.

fault.title: Two calls on one screen
fault.symptom: A 200 OK is on the screen and the phone still rings.
fault.log:
INVITE Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com CSeq: 1 INVITE branch=z9hG4bK7766as01
SIP/2.0 200 OK Call-ID: other-call@example.com CSeq: 1 INVITE branch=z9hG4bK7766as01
choices: The 200 belongs to a different Call-ID
The To tag is optional on every request
fault.why: Call-ID a84b4c76e66710@example.com and Call-ID other-call@example.com are two dialogs.
fault.cause: The success response was matched by branch habit and not by Call-ID.
fault.fix: Pair the 200 to the INVITE only when Call-ID, CSeq, and the Via branch agree. Then look for the end-to-end ACK on that same Call-ID.

lessons.title: Status codes you will actually see
lessons.summary: Read provisional and final codes from RFC 3261 section 21, and keep 422 with RFC 4028.
objectives: Separate provisional codes from final ones
Place 422 with the session-timer RFC
Use 488 for this UA and 606 for a global refusal

illustration.title: Codes for this track
illustration.caption: 422 is Session Interval Too Small from RFC 4028. The other rows are the RFC 3261 section 21 phrases this lesson teaches, plus 606.

paragraphs: 100 Trying is hop by hop and means this hop has the INVITE. 180 Ringing means alerting. 183 Session Progress is the provisional you meet when early media or other progress needs to be signaled before the final answer. None of these three is a final response.

200 OK is the success final response. 302 Moved Temporarily points at a Contact and steps the redirect server out of the dialog. Read the Contact on the 302 and send a new request; the 302 itself is finished once it has been acknowledged as a non-2xx final on that hop.

sections.h: Challenges, busy, cancel, and server errors
paragraphs: 401 Unauthorized is the challenge from a user agent server, commonly a registrar. 407 Proxy Authentication Required is the challenge from a proxy. 408 Request Timeout means the request timed out. 480 Temporarily Unavailable, 486 Busy Here, and 603 Decline are three different refusals: away, busy at this UA, and an explicit decline.

487 Request Terminated is the final response that follows a successful CANCEL of the INVITE. The CANCEL transaction itself completes with 200 OK and CSeq method CANCEL. 500 Server Internal Error and 503 Service Unavailable are server-side failures. 503 often travels with Retry-After. The ACK for every one of these non-2xx finals is hop by hop.

sections.h: 488, 606, and the code that is not in the base list
paragraphs: 488 Not Acceptable Here means this user agent cannot accept the request, often because the session description has no usable overlap. 606 Not Acceptable means the refusal is global: retrying another UA is not expected to help. Keep those two phrases apart when you write the ticket.

422 Session Interval Too Small is defined in RFC 4028, not in the RFC 3261 section 21 list. The response carries Min-SE. The UAC acknowledges the 422 with a hop-by-hop ACK and sends a new INVITE whose session interval is at least that Min-SE. Quoting 422 as a base RFC 3261 status is the mistake this lesson exists to stop.

quiz.q: 487 Request Terminated follows
choices: A successful CANCEL of the INVITE
quiz.why: CANCEL completes with 200 and CSeq CANCEL. The INVITE ends in 487.

quiz.q: 422 Session Interval Too Small is defined in
quiz.why: Keep 422 off the base status-code list. Min-SE comes back in the 422.

quiz.q: 488 compared with 606
choices: 488 is this UA. 606 is a global refusal.
quiz.why: Not Acceptable Here versus Not Acceptable.

quiz.q: 401 differs from 407 because
choices: 401 challenges from a UAS. 407 challenges from a proxy.
quiz.why: Both are authentication challenges. The role that sent them is the difference.

quiz.q: 183 Session Progress is
quiz.why: Early progress stays provisional. 200 is the success final.

quiz.q: The ACK on this ladder's 487 is
choices: Hop by hop, same Via branch as the INVITE
quiz.why: Only the ACK for a 2xx is end to end.

cards.back: Ringing. Provisional alerting.
Session Progress. Provisional, often where early media shows up.
Request Terminated. The INVITE's answer after CANCEL.
Not Acceptable. Global. 488 is only this UA.

fault.title: 422 filed as a base status
fault.symptom: A carrier answers Session-Expires: 90 with 422 and Min-SE: 1800. The ticket says RFC 3261 section 21 defines 422.
fault.log:
INVITE CSeq: 1 INVITE
Session-Expires: 90;refresher=uac
SIP/2.0 422 Session Interval Too Small
Min-SE: 1800
CSeq: 1 INVITE
choices: 422 is the session-timer refusal in RFC 4028
422 means the codec list was empty
Min-SE is an RTP sequence number
The hop-by-hop ACK is omitted after 422
fault.why: The reason phrase is Session Interval Too Small. The base section 21 list is the wrong citation.
fault.cause: The offered session interval is below the far end's Min-SE.
fault.fix: ACK the 422 hop by hop, then send a new INVITE whose Session-Expires is at least the Min-SE in the 422. Cite RFC 4028.

lessons.title: Display filters for SIP and RTP
lessons.summary: Filter the capture with sip, rtp, and sip.Method, and confirm sip.CSeq.method in the SIP display-filter reference.
objectives: Use the display filters this lesson names
Confirm a CSeq field in the Wireshark reference
Read Call-ID from the packet you selected

illustration.title: From file to one transaction
illustration.caption: Display filters narrow what you see. They are not a second copy of the SIP RFC.

paragraphs: The display filters you may type from this lesson are sip, rtp, and sip.Method. A common way to see INVITE requests is sip.CSeq.method == "INVITE". Confirm that field in the Wireshark SIP display-filter reference before you trust it in a ticket. The reference for SIP fields is the page this lesson cites as ws-sip. RTP display fields have their own page, ws-rtp.

sip.Method is the safe method field when you want the request method. This lesson does not invent other field names. If a blog names a filter you have not found on those two reference pages, leave it out of the write-up until you confirm it there.

sections.h: What you read after the filter hits
paragraphs: Select one packet and read the SIP headers in order: Call-ID, CSeq, Via branch, To tag. The filter got you to the packet. The match rules from the ladder lesson decide whether the next packet is the same transaction.

rtp shows the media packets. SIP showing a 200 OK with an m= line does not mean those RTP packets are in the capture. When the call is silent, keep the SIP filter long enough to read the negotiated address and port, then use the rtp display filter to see whether media arrived. Cite the RTP reference for RTP fields and the SIP reference for SIP fields.

paragraphs: debug ccsip messages is a Cisco IOS voice command. Operators use it on IOS voice, including CUBE, to print the SIP messages the stack sent and received. The basic CUBE SIP configuration guide is the product context for that IOS voice role. The bytes after Sent or Received are SIP, so you read them with RFC 3261.

The debug line itself is not a SIP header and not an RFC. Strip the IOS prefix, then dissect the SIP start line. A synthetic lab print is labeled synthetic. A real customer log does not belong in this lesson.

debug voip ccapi inout is a long-standing IOS voice debug for the call-control API. Operators run it beside debug ccsip messages when they need the setup and disconnect indications the voice application saw. Those lines are IOS debug output. They are not a SIP method and they are not defined by RFC 3261.

Use ccapi to see that IOS created or tore down a call leg. Use the ccsip SIP text to see the INVITE, the status code, and the SDP. When the two disagree, believe the SIP message for protocol questions and the ccapi line for what the IOS call-control API did with that leg.

lessons.title: 488 codecs and 422 session timers
lessons.summary: 488 is this UA refusing the session description. 422 is a session interval below Min-SE.
objectives: Read 488 as an offer/answer refusal at this UA
Retry 422 with a large enough session interval
Keep telephone-event in the overlap you meant to keep

illustration.title: Two finals that look like media failed
illustration.caption: They are different requests to the next INVITE.
rows: This UA rejects the session description
A new offer this UA can accept, or stop
Refusal is global, not just this UA
A different offer, not a different UA hop
New INVITE with Session-Expires at least Min-SE

paragraphs: 488 Not Acceptable Here often means the codec or the rest of the SDP was refused by this user agent. RFC 3261 names the status. RFC 3264 is the offer/answer model: the answer may keep a subset of the offered payloads, and an empty overlap of usable media is a failure. 606 would mean the problem is global rather than local to this UA.

PCMU payload 0 and PCMA payload 8 are static names from RFC 3551. telephone-event is the RFC 4733 name for named telephone events, including DTMF. If the answer keeps PCMU and drops PCMA, the call can still proceed. If the answer has no shared audio codec, expect 488 from this UA instead of a 200 OK.

sections.h: 422 is the timer, not the codec
paragraphs: RFC 4028 defines 422 Session Interval Too Small. The UAS sends Min-SE. A synthetic example in this lesson uses Session-Expires: 90 on the first INVITE and Min-SE: 1800 on the 422. 1800 is an example value for the drill, not a universal carrier rule.

ACK that 422 hop by hop, on the INVITE's Via branch. Then send a new INVITE, new branch, next CSeq, with Session-Expires at least the Min-SE you were given. Leaving the codec list alone is the point: 422 did not say the codecs were unacceptable.
On 488, change the offer. Confirm telephone-event is still there if DTMF has to survive. On 422, change the session interval. Doing both in one new INVITE hides which fix worked.
Early offer puts the SDP in the INVITE. The 200 OK carries the answer. A 488 carries no accepted answer. Read the code before you read a packet capture for RTP that the refusal means will not start.

illustration.caption: The first three stop before a SIP status. The fourth is SIP.

paragraphs: Certificate name mismatch, an untrusted CA, and a TLS version the peer will not accept all fail in the handshake. You get no SIP status code from the far end, because the SIP message was never delivered. Say handshake in the ticket, and name which of the three you checked.

Teams Direct Routing requires TLS 1.2 or newer. The OPTIONS and certificate troubleshooting page is the operational source for that requirement. A stack that offers only an older version fails before OPTIONS or INVITE exists on the wire as SIP.

sections.h: Contact must be an FQDN toward Teams
paragraphs: When the handshake succeeds, Direct Routing still requires an FQDN in Contact. An address literal in Contact is answered with 403. The Direct Routing SIP protocol page is the source for that rule. This lab uses sip.pstnhub.microsoft.com as the Teams SIP target and sbc.example.com as the synthetic SBC name.

The certificate name has to match the name you presented. A certificate for a different name is the mismatch case, even if the CA is one you trust. Fix the name, the trust anchor, or the version before you rewrite SDP.

OPTIONS is the liveness request from RFC 3261 section 11. Toward Teams it rides the TLS session you just proved. A synthetic 200 in this lesson means the handshake worked and the peer answered. It is not a captured production packet.
If OPTIONS never leaves the SBC, stay on the handshake. If OPTIONS is answered and the INVITE returns 403, read Contact. Those are different faults and they do not share one fix.

lessons.title: Read an RFC header before you cite it
lessons.summary: Number, category, and Obsoletes or Updates. The RFC Editor header beats a remembered month.
objectives: Read number, category, and Obsoletes or Updates
Keep 422 and 2xx ACK with the RFCs that define them
Leave publication months to the header

illustration.title: The header, top to bottom
illustration.caption: Open the document on the RFC Editor site. Copy the relationship words that are printed there.

layers.name: Category
layers.detail: Standards Track, BCP, Informational, and the rest

layers.name: Obsoletes / Updates
layers.detail: Replacement versus a correction that leaves the base in force

paragraphs: An RFC header gives you the number and the category. RFC 3261 is Standards Track and it is still the base SIP specification. RFC 6881 is the Best Current Practice for emergency calling services. Category is a fact on the header, not a compliment you add in a ticket.

Point at rfc-editor.org for the document you are citing. RFC 5411 is this library's hitchhiker's guide to the SIP specification family. A guide can lag. The header of the specific RFC is the row you quote.

SDP in this library moved from RFC 4566 to RFC 8866. The header on RFC 8866 is where you confirm the Obsoletes line. ICE in this library is RFC 8445, which moved from RFC 5245. STUN in this library is RFC 8489, which moved from RFC 5389. TURN in this library is RFC 8656, which moved from RFC 5766. If a still newer RFC obsoletes one of those and this edition does not cite it, the RFC Editor banner wins.

RFC 6026 corrects transaction handling for 2xx responses to INVITE. Read its header for the Updates line. It is not a replacement of RFC 3261. RFC 4028 is where 422 lives. It is not an Obsoletes of the section 21 list; it is an extension you cite beside the base protocol.
This lesson does not state publication months. The header prints the date. If you need a date in a design record, copy it from rfc-editor.org for that number on the day you looked.

A timeline of a call is still Call-ID and CSeq. A timeline of a specification is number, category, and whether the header says Obsoletes or Updates. Mixing those two timelines is how a ticket cites a blog instead of the document.
